7.about: Beethoven’s Op. 7 was the longest sonata he had yet written and, after the Hammerklavier, remains one of his most expansive. The first movement, in a vigorous 6/8, is driven by pulsing repeated notes and is full of brilliant, orchestral passagework; it seems always to be pressing forward. The Largo, con gran espressione, in C major, is the heart of the work: its phrases are separated by long silences so that the music seems to speak, pause and reflect, and its dramatic middle section moves to remote keys before the calm returns. The third movement, simply marked Allegro, is a minuet-like piece whose trio, in E-flat minor, is a shadowy stream of triplets. The finale is a leisurely, affectionate rondo, Poco allegretto e grazioso, with a violent C-minor episode of rushing notes that briefly threatens the good humour. The work’s scale, variety and emotional reach show Beethoven claiming for the solo sonata the ambition of a symphony, and its slow movement anticipates the searching Adagios of his later years.
7.ctx: Composed in 1796–97 and published in 1797 by Artaria, Op. 7 was issued alone, not as part of a set — a sign that Beethoven considered it a major work. It was dedicated to Countess Babette (Anna Louise Barbara) von Keglevics, his piano pupil, to whom he later dedicated the First Piano Concerto after her marriage to Prince Innocenzo Odescalchi. Early publishers called it ‘Grande Sonate’, and a nineteenth-century nickname, ‘Die Verliebte’ (The Maiden in Love), may refer to rumours of Beethoven’s affection for his pupil. Beethoven was touring in 1796 — to Prague, Dresden, Leipzig and Berlin — and his growing reputation as a composer rather than just a pianist is reflected in the confidence of this work. Its long silences in the Largo are among the earliest examples of Beethoven using rests as expressive events.

A solemn movement in which silence is as eloquent as sound.
A minuet-like movement with a turbulent, shadowy trio.
A warm, flowing rondo with a stormy C-minor episode.
facts: It was the first of his sonatas to be published on its own rather than in a set.
The dedicatee, Babette von Keglevics, also received the dedication of the First Piano Concerto.
Henle rates it level 8, the highest of the pre-1800 sonatas.

13.about: The ‘Pathétique’ is one of Beethoven’s most famous sonatas, and deservedly so. It opens with a weighty Grave introduction, full of dramatic dotted rhythms and sighing phrases, then launches into a stormy Allegro di molto e con brio with a pounding tremolo bass. The Grave returns twice within the Allegro, at the start of the development and before the coda, binding introduction and movement into a single drama — an innovation that influenced later composers. The Adagio cantabile in A-flat major is a noble, songful rondo whose main theme resembles the slow movement of Mozart’s C-minor Sonata K. 457. The finale, a restless Rondo in C minor, shares a melodic contour with the first movement’s second theme, giving the whole work unity. The sonata’s intensity, emotional directness and virtuosity made it a sensation among Beethoven’s contemporaries. The sonata’s structure is tightly unified. The Grave’s rising and falling motifs reappear in the Allegro’s themes, and the finale’s main theme shares its shape with the first movement’s second subject, giving the three movements a sense of shared material. The Allegro’s tremolo bass, marked with rapid repeated octaves, creates an orchestral rumble that was new in piano writing. The Adagio’s warmth, set between two stormy movements, provides essential relief, and its gradual build-up of decoration shows Beethoven’s mastery of variation within a simple rondo.
13.ctx: Composed in 1797–98 and published in Vienna in 1799, the sonata was dedicated to Prince Karl von Lichnowsky, Beethoven’s patron and host in his early Vienna years. The title ‘Grande Sonate pathétique’ appeared on the first edition, probably with Beethoven’s approval. Moscheles, who later became a friend of Beethoven, recalled that as a boy he was forbidden by his teacher to play this ‘eccentric’ music, which he secretly copied. The sonata’s dramatic C-minor style became a model for Romantic composers, and it remains one of the most frequently played of all Beethoven’s works. The sonata appeared during a period of intense activity for Beethoven, alongside the Op. 18 quartets and the First Symphony. Its title and dramatic style made it one of his most popular works during his lifetime, and it was widely arranged and imitated. Its C-minor intensity and slow introduction influenced Romantic sonatas by composers such as Schubert, Mendelssohn and Chopin. It remains among the most performed and recorded of all his works, and a rite of passage for advanced piano students.

Ignaz Moscheles recalled being forbidden to play it as a student because it was considered too eccentric.
Henle lists it at ABRSM Grade 8/ARSM level.

15.about: A bright, festive concerto with trumpets and timpani. The first movement is expansive and brilliant, with a military flavour and virtuosic piano writing. The Largo in A-flat major is a long, lyrical dialogue between piano and clarinet. The rondo finale, Allegro scherzando, is full of high spirits and syncopation. The first movement’s themes are energetic and bright, with a march-like character. The piano enters with a new theme, rather than repeating the orchestra’s music, and dazzles with rapid scales and arpeggios. The Largo’s long melodic lines and dialogue with the clarinet create an intimate atmosphere, while the rondo’s syncopated theme and brilliant piano writing bring the work to a joyful close.
15.ctx: Although numbered first, the concerto was written after the Second Concerto. Beethoven revised it several times. He wrote three cadenzas for the first movement in later years, one of them very long. It was dedicated to Princess Barbara Odescalchi (née Babette von Keglevics), his former pupil. Beethoven premiered the concerto himself, probably in 1795 in Vienna, and played it in Prague in 1798. It was published in 1801 by Mollo. The concerto established Beethoven as a composer of concertos in the tradition of Mozart.
parts: A grand, military-flavoured opening with brilliant piano writing.
A serene, song-like movement with prominent clarinet.

Beethoven wrote three different cadenzas for the first movement.

16.about: A quintet for piano, oboe, clarinet, horn and bassoon, modelled on Mozart’s quintet for the same combination, K. 452.
16.ctx: According to Ferdinand Ries, Beethoven improvised a long cadenza at one performance, irritating the wind players who were waiting to come in.
parts: A slow introduction and a genial Allegro.
facts: It is modelled on Mozart’s K. 452.
Beethoven also arranged it for piano quartet.

19.about: Beethoven’s earliest surviving piano concerto, which he revised several times. It is lighter and more Mozartian than his later concertos, with a graceful first movement, a hymn-like Adagio ending with a recitative, and a rondo with a cheeky syncopated theme. The first movement’s orchestral introduction is long and elegant, and the piano’s entry brings a new, more intimate theme. The Adagio, in E-flat major, is one of the most expressive slow movements of Beethoven’s early period, with a long recitative-like passage for the piano at the end, marked ‘con gran espressione’. The finale’s theme, with its off-beat accents, gives the movement a rustic, playful character, and Beethoven originally wrote a different finale, now known as the Rondo in B-flat, WoO 6.
19.ctx: Begun in Bonn around 1787–89, the concerto was a vehicle for Beethoven’s early career as a pianist in Vienna. He published it after the First Concerto in 1801. Beethoven himself described it as not one of his best works. Beethoven played the concerto at his public debut in Vienna in March 1795. He revised it several times, and wrote a new cadenza for the first movement in 1809. It was published in 1801 by Hoffmeister, alongside the First Symphony and the Septet. Its scoring, without clarinets, trumpets or timpani, reflects its early origins.
parts: A slow, deeply expressive movement ending with a recitative.
A playful rondo with a hopping, syncopated theme.
19.sc: Piano, flute, 2 oboes, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, strings
facts: It is his earliest surviving piano concerto.

20.about: A sunny, six-movement divertimento for clarinet, horn, bassoon, violin, viola, cello and double bass. It was one of Beethoven’s most popular works in his lifetime.
20.ctx: Beethoven later became irritated by its popularity, reportedly wishing it could be destroyed. It inspired Schubert’s Octet.
parts: A slow introduction and a lively Allegro.
A minuet using the theme of the Sonata Op. 49 No. 2.
Andante con moto alla marcia – Presto

21.about: Beethoven’s First Symphony looks back to Haydn and Mozart while announcing a new voice. Its very first chord is a dominant seventh that resolves to F major rather than the home key of C — a harmonic surprise that caused comment in its day — and the slow introduction takes its time to find its way home. The Allegro con brio that follows is compact, energetic and driven by a crisp, rising theme, with prominent, sometimes brassy wind writing that critics found noisy. The Andante cantabile con moto begins with a gentle fugal entry in the second violins and features soft timpani strokes, unusual in a slow movement. The third movement is labelled Menuetto but is really a fast scherzo, with a trio of sustained wind chords against rippling violins. The finale opens with a famous joke: the violins creep up the scale, one note at a time, as if unsure of themselves, before bursting into a sparkling, Haydnesque Allegro. The symphony is short and cheerful, but its wit, energy and bold wind writing mark it as the work of a composer who intended to go beyond his models.
21.ctx: The symphony was premiered on 2 April 1800 at the Burgtheater in Vienna, at the first public concert Beethoven organised for his own benefit. The programme also included a Mozart symphony, excerpts from Haydn’s Creation, the Septet Op. 20 and a piano concerto played by Beethoven. The Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung praised the symphony’s art, novelty and wealth of ideas, though it complained about the excessive use of wind instruments. It was dedicated to Baron Gottfried van Swieten, a diplomat and music lover who had introduced Mozart and Haydn to the music of Bach and Handel and had written the libretto for Haydn’s Creation. Beethoven was nearly thirty when he completed his First Symphony, relatively late compared with Mozart and Haydn, which reflects the seriousness with which he approached the genre. It was published in 1801 by Hoffmeister & Kühnel in Leipzig.
parts: A slow introduction that starts off-key, then a brisk, confident Allegro.
A graceful movement with gentle fugal entries and soft timpani.
A minuet in name only — really Beethoven’s first symphonic scherzo.

22.about: A confident, four-movement sonata in B-flat major, the summit of Beethoven’s early classical style. The first movement is energetic and brilliant, with a vigorous theme and sparkling passagework. The Adagio con molta espressione in E-flat major is a broad, singing movement in the style of an operatic aria, full of rich harmony. The Menuetto is graceful with a stormy G-minor trio of rushing notes. The finale is a relaxed, songful rondo with a contrapuntal minor-key episode. Beethoven considered this sonata one of his best works of the period. The sonata is often overlooked beside the more dramatic works that surround it, but pianists admire it for its balance and craftsmanship. The first movement’s energetic theme is developed with great resourcefulness, and the Adagio’s long, singing lines require careful control of tone and pedal. The finale’s gentle rondo theme, which returns in varied forms, is balanced by a turbulent minor-key episode full of counterpoint. The work shows Beethoven at ease with the classical sonata, before he began to reshape it.
22.ctx: Composed in 1800 and published in 1802 by Hoffmeister, the sonata was dedicated to Count Johann Georg von Browne. Beethoven offered it to his publisher in a letter, describing it as a sonata that ‘hat sich gewaschen’ — Viennese slang for a first-rate, thoroughly worked piece. It was the last sonata he wrote in the traditional classical mould before beginning to experiment with form in Op. 26 and Op. 27. Beethoven composed it in 1800, the year of the premiere of the First Symphony and the Septet. His letter offering it to the Leipzig publisher Franz Anton Hoffmeister shows his confidence: he asked 20 ducats for it, the same price as the Septet and the First Symphony. It was published in 1802, by which time Beethoven had already moved on to more experimental works.
parts: A broad, singing movement in the style of an operatic aria.
A graceful minuet with a stormy G-minor trio.
A relaxed, songful rondo with a contrapuntal minor-key episode.
facts: Beethoven described it as a sonata that ‘hat sich gewaschen’ (has washed itself), meaning first-class.
It marks the end of his early classical period in the sonatas.
Henle rates it level 7.

23.about: A nervous, terse sonata in three movements. The first movement, Presto in 6/8 time, is quick and restless, with a driving rhythm and sudden dynamic contrasts. The middle movement, Andante scherzoso, più Allegretto, is a half-humorous piece in A major with fugal touches, replacing a traditional slow movement. The finale, Allegro molto, is a quick rondo with a hint of melancholy, ending quietly.
23.ctx: Originally intended to be published together with the ‘Spring’ Sonata as Op. 23, a printing error (the two parts were engraved in different formats) caused the two to be published separately in 1801, with the ‘Spring’ becoming Op. 24. Both were dedicated to Count Moritz von Fries, a wealthy banker and patron of the arts. The sonata’s dark, restless character contrasts sharply with its sunny companion.
facts: It was meant to be published together with the ‘Spring’ Sonata.
It has no true slow movement.
The dedicatee, Count Moritz von Fries, also received the Seventh Symphony.

24.about: One of Beethoven’s sunniest works, and his first four-movement violin sonata. The violin opens with a long, flowing melody over rippling piano accompaniment. The Adagio molto espressivo is songful and calm, with decorated melodies. The tiny scherzo includes a famous joke where the violin lags a beat behind the piano, creating a comic mismatch. The rondo finale is gentle and happy, with a warm, lyrical theme. The sonata’s lyricism and charm have made it one of the most popular violin sonatas ever written.
24.ctx: The nickname ‘Spring’ was added after Beethoven’s death, probably because of the work’s fresh, lyrical character. Composed in 1800–01, it was written during the same period as the Second Symphony and the Op. 27 sonatas. It remains one of the most frequently performed of Beethoven’s violin sonatas.
parts: A flowing, lyrical movement that opens with a violin song.
A tiny scherzo where the violin seems to lag behind.
facts: The scherzo’s rhythmic joke has the violin sounding a beat behind the piano.
The nickname ‘Spring’ is not Beethoven’s.
It is his first violin sonata in four movements.

26.about: An unconventional sonata in A-flat major that departs from the usual fast–slow–fast structure. It opens with a set of five variations on a gentle, lyrical theme. The second movement is a brisk scherzo with a smooth trio. The third movement is a funeral march ‘on the death of a hero’, in A-flat minor, with imitations of muffled drum rolls and trumpet calls. The finale is a perpetual-motion Allegro of running semiquavers. The work’s unusual design and its funeral march made it a model for later composers, particularly Chopin, whose own Sonata No. 2 includes a famous funeral march. The sonata’s unusual order — variations, scherzo, funeral march, finale — gives it the character of a suite or a sequence of scenes rather than a classical argument. The variations explore different textures and registers, including a dark minor-key variation. The funeral march’s drum-roll tremolos in the bass and trumpet-like fanfares show Beethoven imitating orchestral sounds on the piano. The perpetual-motion finale, often played fast and light, provides a surprising contrast after the march’s gravity.
26.ctx: Composed in 1800–01 and published in 1802 by Cappi, the sonata was dedicated to Prince Karl von Lichnowsky. The funeral march was so admired that Beethoven orchestrated it in 1815 for the incidental music to Friedrich Duncker’s play Leonore Prohaska (WoO 96), and it was played at his own funeral procession in March 1827. Some scholars suggest it was inspired by the funeral march in Ferdinando Paër’s opera Achille, which Beethoven admired. The sonata was written in 1800–01, when Napoleon’s victories were transforming Europe and the idea of the heroic was in the air. The funeral march foreshadows the Eroica Symphony’s second movement, written a few years later. Chopin, who admired this sonata, is said to have been influenced by its funeral march when writing his own Sonata in B-flat minor, Op. 35.

28.about: A calm, rural-sounding sonata in D major, built over long pedal notes like a drone. The first movement opens with a repeated D in the bass, over which a gentle melody unfolds. The Andante in D minor has a walking bass and a dotted-rhythm middle section; Czerny recalled that Beethoven loved to play it. The Scherzo is humorous, built on repeated single notes. The finale is a rocking, bagpipe-like rondo with a brilliant coda. The nickname ‘Pastoral’ was added by the publisher August Cranz in 1838 and reflects the sonata’s gentle, rustic character. The sonata is spacious and unhurried, with long pedal points giving it a sense of calm. The first movement’s gentle melody unfolds over a steady bass, and its development section builds to a climax before subsiding. The Andante’s walking bass and simple melody give it a folk-like quality. The Scherzo’s repeated single notes create a humorous, rustic effect, while the finale’s rocking bass evokes a bagpipe. The coda, marked Più allegro quasi presto, provides a brilliant ending.
28.ctx: Composed in 1801 and published in 1802 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, the sonata was dedicated to Joseph von Sonnenfels, a prominent Viennese writer and reformer, and professor of political science. Written in the same year as the Moonlight Sonata, it shows the other side of Beethoven at the time: serene and unhurried. It anticipates the mood of his Pastoral Symphony. Composed in 1801, the sonata belongs to the same year as the Second Symphony and the Moonlight Sonata. Its calm character contrasts with the dramatic works around it. It is sometimes seen as a precursor to the Pastoral Symphony, which also evokes rural life. The sonata has been particularly admired by pianists for its lyrical qualities.

A walking-bass march that Beethoven reportedly loved to play.

33.about: Seven short, characterful pieces. Beethoven called them ‘Bagatelles’ (trifles), but they are carefully crafted, with a wide range of moods.
33.ctx: Some of the pieces may have been drafted in Bonn. Their brevity and variety anticipate the Romantic character piece.
facts: The title ‘Bagatelle’ means ‘trifle’.
Some pieces may date from Beethoven’s Bonn years.
Henle rates the pieces between levels 4 and 7.

34.about: An innovative set of variations in which each variation is in a different key and has a different character.
34.ctx: Beethoven offered this set and Op. 35 to his publisher as works in a new style.

35.about: A large set of variations that begins with the bass line alone, gradually building up the theme. It ends with a powerful fugue.
35.ctx: The theme also appears in Beethoven’s ballet The Creatures of Prometheus and in the finale of the Eroica Symphony. Beethoven stressed that these variations were written in a ‘quite new manner’.

36.prem: 5 April 1803, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
36.about: The Second Symphony expands the scale of the First, with a long, dramatic slow introduction that includes a powerful D-minor outburst anticipating the Ninth Symphony. The Allegro con brio is energetic and full of contrasts, with a surging theme first heard in the cellos and basses. The Larghetto is a long, flowing and lyrical slow movement, one of Beethoven’s most beautiful, with a warm melody passed between strings and winds. The third movement is Beethoven’s first symphonic movement explicitly titled Scherzo, playful and full of sudden dynamic contrasts. The finale is witty and explosive, opening with a sudden hiccup-like motif, and includes an extended coda that some early critics found too long. Critics of the time found the symphony bizarre and noisy, but it is now admired for its energy and humour.
36.ctx: Beethoven completed the symphony in Heiligenstadt in 1802, the same autumn he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament, a despairing letter to his brothers about his growing deafness, in which he confessed that only his art had kept him from ending his life. Yet the symphony’s high spirits show none of that crisis. It was premiered on 5 April 1803 at the Theater an der Wien, alongside the Third Piano Concerto and the oratorio Christ on the Mount of Olives, and was dedicated to Prince Karl von Lichnowsky. A critic in the Zeitung für die elegante Welt famously compared it to a ‘hideously writhing, wounded dragon’ that refused to die, bleeding to death in the finale.

37.prem: 5 April 1803, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
37.about: A dramatic concerto in C minor that shows the influence of Mozart’s Concerto No. 24 in the same key. The first movement is powerful and stern, with a dramatic cadenza and a quiet, mysterious coda where the timpani echo the main theme. The Largo moves to the remote key of E major, a distant, luminous slow movement. The rondo ends with a joyful switch to C major. The first movement’s theme, in C minor, is stated quietly by the strings before the full orchestra takes it up. The piano’s entry with rushing scales is dramatic, and the movement’s coda, after the cadenza, is quiet and mysterious. The Largo’s distant key of E major creates a sense of stillness. The finale’s theme, in C minor, is energetic and syncopated, and the switch to C major for the coda brings a joyful end.
37.ctx: At the premiere on 5 April 1803, the piano part was not fully written out. Page-turner Ignaz von Seyfried recalled turning mostly blank pages while Beethoven played from memory, nodding to him when he needed to turn. It was dedicated to Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia, a talented composer and pianist who died in battle in 1806. The concerto was premiered at the same concert as the Second Symphony and the oratorio Christ on the Mount of Olives. It was published in 1804 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie. Beethoven wrote a cadenza for the first movement in 1809, which is still widely played.

43.about: Beethoven’s only full-length ballet. It depicts the Titan Prometheus bringing two statues to life and educating them in the arts. The finale theme was later used in the Eroica Symphony.
43.ctx: The choreography was by Salvatore Viganò. The ballet was a success, with 23 performances in its first two years.

47.about: A concerto-like sonata of great virtuosity and scale. A slow introduction, beginning with the violin alone in rich double stops, leads to a fiery, dramatic Presto in A minor. The middle movement is a set of four virtuosic variations on a lyrical theme in F major, with a serene coda. The finale is a whirling tarantella in 6/8, originally written for the Sonata Op. 30 No. 1. Beethoven described it on the manuscript as ‘written in a very concertante style, quite like a concerto’.
47.ctx: Written for the violinist George Bridgetower, a mixed-race virtuoso of Caribbean and Polish descent, who premiered it with Beethoven on 24 May 1803 in Vienna. Beethoven finished it so late that Bridgetower had to read the violin part from Beethoven’s manuscript. After a quarrel — reportedly over a woman — Beethoven dedicated it to the French violinist Rodolphe Kreutzer, who reportedly never played it and called it unintelligible. Tolstoy named a novella after it, and Janáček wrote a string quartet inspired by Tolstoy’s story.

50.about: A sweet, songful romance for violin and orchestra, with a gently flowing melody.

53.about: The ‘Waldstein’ is a landmark of Beethoven’s heroic style, full of energy and light. It opens with pulsing repeated chords in the bass, pianissimo, that gradually build to a brilliant climax, and the harmony moves quickly through distant keys. The second theme, a chorale-like melody in E major, provides a calm contrast. The movement is expansive and orchestral, with shimmering textures that exploit the wider range of the new pianos. The second movement, marked Introduzione: Adagio molto, is a short, brooding bridge that leads directly into the finale. The Rondo begins with a radiant, bell-like theme over shimmering trills and pedal, gradually building to a grand climax, and ends with a dazzling Prestissimo coda that includes octave glissandos. The sonata’s scale and brilliance make it one of the most demanding in the repertoire. Pianists often describe the Waldstein as a study in sonority: the opening requires perfectly even repeated chords, and the finale’s long pedal markings, which blend harmonies over the melody, are meant to create a luminous haze.
53.ctx: Composed in 1803–04 and published in 1805 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, the sonata was dedicated to Count Ferdinand von Waldstein, Beethoven’s early patron in Bonn. Waldstein had sent Beethoven to Vienna with the words that he would receive ‘the spirit of Mozart from the hands of Haydn’. Beethoven wrote the sonata after receiving a new piano from the French maker Érard in 1803, which had a wider range and a different sound. The original slow movement was a longer Andante, which a friend thought made the sonata too long; Beethoven replaced it with the Introduzione and published the Andante separately as the ‘Andante favori’ (WoO 57). The sonata stands at the start of Beethoven’s ‘heroic’ period, alongside the Eroica Symphony.

A short, mysterious bridge leading directly into the finale.
A radiant, bell-like theme over trills, ending in a brilliant coda.

54.about: An enigmatic two-movement sonata overshadowed by its neighbours, the Waldstein and Appassionata. The first movement, In tempo d’un menuetto, alternates a courtly minuet with blunt, stomping octave passages, as if two different characters were arguing. The second movement, Allegretto, is a relentless two-part invention in perpetual motion that accelerates into a Più allegro coda. Its concentration and experimental character make it a fascinating, if puzzling, work. Its brevity and experiments have led pianists to treat it as a hidden gem, and performers such as Sviatoslav Richter championed it.
54.ctx: Composed in 1804 and published in 1806 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, the sonata has no dedication. Its compact size and unusual structure contrast with the grand sonatas around it. Some commentators, including Tovey, admired its subtlety, while others found it strange. Its experiments with contrast and continuous motion point toward Beethoven’s later concentration of material. Beethoven wrote it in the same year as the Triple Concerto and the Appassionata.
parts: A courtly minuet interrupted by rough, stomping octaves.
A continuous two-part invention that accelerates into a Più allegro coda.
facts: It is sandwiched between the Waldstein and Appassionata sonatas.
The second movement is a perpetual-motion two-part invention.
Henle lists it at ABRSM ARSM level.

55.prem: Private 1804 at Prince Lobkowitz’s; public 7 April 1805, Theater an der Wien
55.about: The ‘Eroica’ is a revolutionary work that redefined the symphony. Its first movement is enormous, nearly as long as an entire Haydn symphony, and is launched by two sharp E-flat chords. The main theme, a simple arpeggio, is soon undermined by a strange C-sharp in the cellos, and the movement unfolds as a drama of conflict, with harsh, syncopated dissonances in the development and a new theme in E minor. Famously, the horn enters with the main theme just before the recapitulation, apparently too early — a moment that startled early listeners. The second movement is a solemn funeral march in C minor, with a noble major-key middle section and a fugal climax, ending with the theme disintegrating. The scherzo is a whispering, driving movement with a trio for three horns, the first time a symphony used three horns. The finale is a set of variations on a theme from Beethoven’s ballet The Creatures of Prometheus, beginning with the bare bass line and building to a triumphant coda.
55.ctx: Beethoven originally planned to title the symphony ‘Bonaparte’, in admiration of Napoleon as a champion of revolutionary ideals. According to Ferdinand Ries, when Beethoven heard in May 1804 that Napoleon had declared himself emperor, he flew into a rage, exclaiming that Napoleon was just an ordinary man who would trample on the rights of others, and tore the title page in two. The surviving manuscript copy shows the words ‘intitolata Bonaparte’ scratched out so violently that the paper is torn. The published title reads ‘Sinfonia eroica, composta per festeggiare il sovvenire di un grand’uomo’ (Heroic Symphony, composed to celebrate the memory of a great man). The symphony was first performed privately at Prince Lobkowitz’s palace in 1804, and publicly on 7 April 1805 at the Theater an der Wien. It was dedicated to Lobkowitz, who had bought the rights to it for a period.
parts: Two sharp chords launch a vast, conflicted drama.
A funeral march with a noble major-key middle section and a fugal climax.
A whispering, driving scherzo with a trio for three horns.
Variations on a theme from The Creatures of Prometheus, ending in triumph.

56.prem: Probably 1804, private; public May 1808, Augarten, Vienna
56.about: A unique concerto for piano trio (violin, cello and piano) and orchestra. The cello often leads, playing high in its range. The work is genial and warm rather than dramatic, with a short, songful Largo and a lively polonaise finale. The first movement is broad and sunny, with the soloists trading themes. The cello introduces each new theme, and the violin and piano follow. The Largo is short and songful, led by the cello, and leads directly into the finale, a lively polonaise-rondo with a contrasting minor-key episode. The work’s unusual scoring creates a unique texture, combining chamber music intimacy with orchestral grandeur.
56.ctx: Beethoven may have written the piano part for his pupil Archduke Rudolph, then a teenager, which may explain why it is less demanding than the string parts. It was dedicated to Prince Lobkowitz. It was premiered publicly in May 1808 at the Augarten in Vienna. The concerto was composed in 1803–04, alongside the Eroica Symphony and the Waldstein Sonata. It was published in 1807 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie. The concerto’s difficult cello part may have been written for Anton Kraft, a renowned cellist in Prince Lobkowitz’s orchestra. It is often overshadowed by Beethoven’s other concertos, but has become more popular in recent years, with performances by famous trios.
parts: A broad, sunny movement where the soloists trade themes.
A short, songful movement led by the cello, leading into the finale.
56.sc: Piano, violin, cello, flute, 2 oboes, 2 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 horns, 2 trumpets, timpani, strings
facts: It is the only concerto Beethoven wrote for more than one soloist.

57.about: The ‘Appassionata’ is one of the most intense works in the piano repertoire. The first movement opens with whispered arpeggios in unison, followed by ominous four-note knocks that recall the Fifth Symphony, and builds to explosive climaxes. The second theme, a lyrical melody derived from the first, provides only brief relief. The development and coda are among the most turbulent passages Beethoven wrote. The second movement is a set of serene variations on a chorale-like theme in D-flat major, which ends with a crashing diminished-seventh chord that leads without a break into the finale. The finale, Allegro ma non troppo, is a relentless, whirling perpetual motion that ends in a ferocious Presto coda. The sonata’s dramatic power made it one of Beethoven’s most celebrated works. Its demands on power and stamina make it a cornerstone of the virtuoso repertoire.
57.ctx: Composed in 1804–05 and published in 1807 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, the sonata was dedicated to Count Franz von Brunsvik, a close friend of Beethoven and brother of Therese and Josephine Brunsvik. The nickname ‘Appassionata’ was added by the publisher Cranz in 1838. According to Ferdinand Ries, Beethoven composed the finale during a long walk in the countryside, humming and howling as he went. Beethoven reportedly considered it his greatest sonata until he wrote the Hammerklavier. Lenin is said to have admired it greatly. It was published in 1807 and remains among the most performed of his sonatas.
parts: Whispered arpeggios and thunderous outbursts in a vast sonata form.
Serene variations on a chorale-like theme, broken off by a crashing chord.

58.prem: March 1807, Palais Lobkowitz (private); 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien (public)
58.about: A lyrical, poetic concerto that begins unusually with the solo piano, quietly stating the theme before the orchestra answers in a distant key (B major). The short slow movement is a dialogue between stern strings and a soft, pleading piano, often compared to Orpheus taming the Furies. The finale bursts in with rhythmic energy and begins in the ‘wrong’ key of C major. The first movement’s dialogue between piano and orchestra is intimate and lyrical, and the piano often leads rather than follows. The slow movement is short but deeply dramatic: the strings play stern, unison phrases, and the piano responds with soft, pleading melodies, gradually calming the strings. The finale is lively and full of rhythmic energy, with the trumpets and timpani entering for the first time in the concerto.
58.ctx: Beethoven played the solo at the premiere concert on 22 December 1808 — his last appearance as soloist in a concerto. The concerto was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph. It was neglected for years after Beethoven’s death until Mendelssohn revived it in 1836. The concerto was one of the works premiered at the 1808 concert. Beethoven composed it in 1805–06, alongside the Fourth Symphony and the Violin Concerto. Its lyrical style and innovations influenced later composers, including Brahms. The concerto’s opening, with the piano alone, was unprecedented in a classical concerto.
parts: The piano opens alone, gently; the orchestra replies in B major.
Harsh strings and a soft, pleading piano in dialogue.
A bright, rhythmic rondo that begins in the ‘wrong’ key.

facts: It was Beethoven’s last public appearance as a concerto soloist.

60.about: The Fourth Symphony is a buoyant, lyrical work that emerges from a mysterious, shadowy introduction into brilliant light. The Adagio introduction begins in B-flat minor with hushed, sustained notes and wandering harmonies, before a sudden crescendo launches the joyous Allegro vivace. The slow movement, Adagio in E-flat major, is serene and singing, with a persistent dotted rhythm that gives it a gentle pulse, and a famous clarinet solo. The third movement, Allegro vivace, is a lively scherzo whose trio is heard twice, a structure Beethoven would use again in the Seventh Symphony. The finale, Allegro ma non troppo, is a whirlwind of rapid notes, with a famous and difficult bassoon solo, ending with a humorous slowdown before the final dash.
60.ctx: Beethoven wrote the symphony in the summer of 1806 while staying with Prince Lichnowsky at his castle in Silesia, where he met Count Franz von Oppersdorff, who commissioned it. It was premiered privately in March 1807 at the palace of Prince Lobkowitz. The symphony is often overshadowed by its neighbours, the Eroica and the Fifth. Schumann is said to have called it ‘a slender Greek maiden between two Norse giants’. Weber, in a satirical review, mocked its introduction as having ‘three or four notes per quarter of an hour’. It uses only a single flute, one of the smallest orchestras of any Beethoven symphony. It premiered publicly in 1808.
parts: A hushed, uncertain introduction erupts into a joyous Allegro.
A gentle, singing movement over a steady dotted pulse.
A lively scherzo whose trio is heard twice.
A breathless, humorous finale with a famous bassoon solo.

61.prem: 23 December 1806, Theater an der Wien (Franz Clement, soloist)
61.about: One of the greatest violin concertos. It opens with four quiet timpani strokes, a motif that runs through the first movement. The mood is serene and lyrical rather than virtuosic. The Larghetto is a calm set of variations, and the finale a lively rondo with hunting-horn calls. The first movement is long and expansive, with a leisurely orchestral introduction. The timpani motif appears throughout, sometimes in the strings or winds. The violin enters with a rising line and plays mostly high, lyrical melodies. The Larghetto is a set of variations on a simple theme, with the violin decorating the melody. A short cadenza leads into the rondo, which has a lively, dancing theme with hunting-horn calls.
61.ctx: Written for violinist Franz Clement, who reportedly sight-read parts of it at the premiere on 23 December 1806. It was rarely played until Joseph Joachim revived it in 1844, aged 12, under Mendelssohn. Beethoven also arranged it as a piano concerto (Op. 61a), with a cadenza featuring the timpani. It was dedicated to Stephan von Breuning, Beethoven’s childhood friend. Beethoven composed the concerto in 1806, the same year as the Fourth Symphony and the Razumovsky Quartets. It was published in 1808 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie. Clement’s performance at the premiere included his own showpiece, played with the violin upside down. The concerto was not immediately successful, and it was rarely performed until Joachim’s revival. Cadenzas have been written by Joachim, Kreisler and many others.

Gentle variations leading straight into the finale.
A dance-like rondo with hunting-horn flavour.

62.about: A dark, dramatic overture that portrays the Roman hero Coriolanus, torn between pride and his mother’s pleas. It ends with a quiet, dying fall.
62.ctx: Written for a revival of Heinrich von Collin’s tragedy Coriolan, not Shakespeare’s play.

67.prem: 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
67.about: The most famous symphony ever written. Its four-note motif (short-short-short-long) opens the work and permeates the whole symphony, which moves from C-minor struggle to C-major triumph. The first movement is concise and relentless, built almost entirely from the motif, with a brief, plaintive oboe cadenza in the recapitulation. The second movement, Andante con moto, is a set of double variations alternating a gentle theme with a martial fanfare. The third movement is a spectral scherzo with a gruff, fugal trio for the cellos and basses. The scherzo returns quietly and leads without a break, through a suspenseful transition over a timpani pedal, into the blazing finale. The finale adds piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones to the orchestra — among the first symphonies to use trombones — and is a triumphant march. The scherzo’s ghost returns before the coda, adding to the drama.
67.ctx: The symphony was premiered on 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien, in a marathon four-hour concert in an unheated hall that also included the Pastoral Symphony, the Fourth Piano Concerto, the Choral Fantasy, parts of the Mass in C, and the concert aria ‘Ah! perfido’. The concert was poorly rehearsed and the audience was cold and tired. E.T.A. Hoffmann’s 1810 review in the Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung hailed it as a masterpiece of Romanticism. The idea that the opening depicts ‘fate knocking at the door’ comes from Schindler, whose reports are unreliable. During World War II, the opening motif was used by the Allied forces as a symbol of victory, because its rhythm matches the Morse code for the letter V. The symphony’s motif has been adapted countless times in popular culture.

68.prem: 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
68.about: Beethoven’s nature symphony, in five movements with descriptive titles. The first movement depicts the awakening of cheerful feelings on arrival in the countryside, with gentle, repeated patterns. The second is a scene by the brook, with murmuring strings and a famous cadenza of birdsong: nightingale (flute), quail (oboe) and cuckoo (clarinet). The third is a merry gathering of country folk, with a rustic dance and a clumsy village band. The fourth is a dramatic thunderstorm that sweeps in and gradually passes, using piccolo and timpani for the first time in the symphony. The finale is the shepherd’s song of thanksgiving, built on a yodel-like theme. The last three movements are played without a break.
68.ctx: Beethoven loved long walks in the countryside around Vienna and often composed outdoors. He wrote that the symphony was ‘more the expression of feeling than painting’ (‘Mehr Ausdruck der Empfindung als Malerei’), to avoid being seen as writing mere imitation. It was premiered on 22 December 1808, in the same concert as the Fifth Symphony. The symphony helped inspire later programme music, from Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique to Liszt’s symphonic poems. It featured in Disney’s film Fantasia (1940), with mythological scenes. Beethoven sketched birdsong in his notebooks during country walks.

69.about: The first cello sonata in which cello and piano are truly equal. It opens with the cello alone singing a noble theme. A syncopated, off-balance scherzo follows, then a brief Adagio cantabile leads into a joyful finale.
69.ctx: Written in the same period as the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies. On the copy for Baron Ignaz von Gleichenstein, the dedicatee, Beethoven wrote ‘Inter lacrimas et luctum’ (amid tears and sorrow). Gleichenstein was a close friend and helped Beethoven with business affairs.

72.prem: 20 November 1805 (as Leonore), Theater an der Wien; final version 23 May 1814, Kärntnertortheater
72.about: Beethoven’s only opera. Leonore disguises herself as a man, Fidelio, to rescue her husband Florestan, a political prisoner. It celebrates married love, freedom and justice.
72.ctx: The first performance, in front of an audience of French officers occupying Vienna, was a failure. Beethoven revised the opera twice and wrote four overtures for it.
parts: The overture to the final 1814 version.
A canon quartet in Act I.

73.about: Beethoven’s last and grandest piano concerto. It opens with the piano playing flourishes over orchestral chords before the main theme appears. The first movement is on a grand, military scale, with no cadenza (Beethoven wrote in the score that the pianist should not add one). The slow movement is a serene hymn in B major that leads without a break into the jubilant rondo, which has a dancing, syncopated theme. The first movement’s grand opening, with piano cadenzas over orchestral chords, is one of the most famous in the concerto repertoire. The Adagio’s hymn-like melody, in B major, is played by muted strings, and the piano enters with a delicate, ornamented line. At the end of the Adagio, the piano quietly previews the finale’s theme before bursting into the rondo.
73.ctx: Composed in 1809 while Napoleon besieged and occupied Vienna. The nickname ‘Emperor’ was not Beethoven’s and was probably added by the English publisher Johann Baptist Cramer. Beethoven was too deaf to perform it himself. It was premiered on 28 November 1811 at the Leipzig Gewandhaus, with Friedrich Schneider as soloist. Carl Czerny gave the Vienna premiere in 1812. Beethoven was unable to perform the concerto himself due to his deafness. It was the last concerto he completed, though he started a sixth piano concerto in 1815, which he abandoned. The concerto was published in 1810–11 by Breitkopf & Härtel and Clementi. It was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven’s pupil and patron.

74.about: A warm, expansive quartet named for the harp-like pizzicato arpeggios in the first movement. The Adagio is deeply lyrical, the scherzo driving and relentless, recalling the Fifth Symphony, and the finale a set of six variations on a simple theme.
74.ctx: Written in 1809, the year Napoleon’s army occupied Vienna. The nickname ‘Harp’ was not Beethoven’s. It was dedicated to Prince Lobkowitz and published in 1810.

78.about: A short, affectionate two-movement sonata in the rare key of F-sharp major. A brief Adagio cantabile introduction, only four bars long, leads to a warm, lyrical Allegro ma non troppo. The second movement, Allegro vivace, is playful and quick, with bright, rocking figures and sudden key changes. The sonata’s intimacy and charm make it a favourite among pianists, though its key signature with six sharps can be challenging to read. Its two movements are both in F-sharp major, a rare choice for Beethoven, and the sonata’s intimate tone suggests a private, affectionate gift. The finale’s quick, off-beat accents and sudden turns demand a light touch and precise rhythm.
78.ctx: Composed in 1809 and published in 1810 by Breitkopf & Härtel, the sonata was dedicated to Countess Therese von Brunsvik, a close friend of Beethoven. Czerny reported that Beethoven was particularly fond of this sonata and considered it better than the Moonlight Sonata. It was written in the same year as the Emperor Concerto and the Les Adieux Sonata, during Napoleon’s occupation of Vienna. Therese von Brunsvik was one of Beethoven’s closest friends; some scholars once proposed her as the ‘Immortal Beloved’, though her sister Josephine is now considered a more likely candidate.

79.about: A light, compact sonata described on its first edition as a ‘sonatine’. The first movement is a German dance with cuckoo-like hand crossings. The G-minor Andante is a gently swaying barcarolle, and the brief finale is cheerful and lighthearted. Its easy charm contrasts sharply with the turmoil of the time it was written. The first movement’s hand crossings imitate a cuckoo’s call, and its lively dance rhythms make it one of the most approachable of Beethoven’s mature sonatas. The Andante’s gentle, rocking melody in thirds evokes a Venetian gondola song, and the finale’s short, cheerful theme is repeated with charming variations.
79.ctx: Composed in 1809 and published in 1810 by Breitkopf & Härtel, the sonata has no dedication. The nickname ‘Cuckoo’ refers to the first movement’s cuckoo-call figures. It was written during Napoleon’s occupation of Vienna, which Beethoven experienced by hiding in his brother’s cellar with pillows over his ears to protect his hearing from the bombardment. The sonata is often taught to intermediate students as a first step towards the larger sonatas. It was composed alongside the Piano Concerto No. 5 and the String Quartet Op. 74, showing Beethoven’s range in that difficult year.

80.prem: 22 December 1808, Theater an der Wien, Vienna
80.about: A unique work for piano, orchestra and chorus. It begins with a long improvisatory piano solo, followed by variations on a theme that anticipates the ‘Ode to Joy’, ending with a chorus.
80.ctx: Written as a finale for Beethoven’s famous 1808 concert, which also premiered the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies.

84.about: A dramatic overture depicting the struggle and triumph of Count Egmont, a hero executed for resisting Spanish oppression. It opens with a sombre introduction and ends with a triumphant ‘Victory Symphony’.
84.ctx: Part of Beethoven’s incidental music for Goethe’s play Egmont. Beethoven greatly admired Goethe, and the two met in Teplitz in 1812.

90.about: A two-movement sonata with German tempo markings instead of Italian, the first in a series of late works where Beethoven used German. The first movement is agitated and emotional, with sudden changes of mood. The second is a long, flowing rondo with an endlessly singing melody, often compared to Schubert. Its lyrical intimacy contrasts sharply with the first movement’s turbulence. The two movements are balanced: the first is compact and dramatic, while the second is long and lyrical, its main theme returning many times with subtle changes. Pianists admire the sonata for its emotional directness and its transitional position between Beethoven’s middle and late styles. The German tempo markings reflect his growing interest in using his native language in music.
90.ctx: Composed in 1814 and published in 1815 by Steiner, the sonata was dedicated to Count Moritz von Lichnowsky, brother of Prince Karl. According to Schindler, Beethoven told the count that the movements represented ‘a struggle between head and heart’ and ‘conversation with the beloved’, referring to the count’s marriage to the singer Josepha Stummer. The sonata was written during the Congress of Vienna, when Beethoven enjoyed great public success. The Congress of Vienna brought many of Europe’s rulers and diplomats to the city, and Beethoven’s music was performed frequently; he later remembered this as the high point of his public fame.

92.about: A symphony driven by rhythm. After a grand, spacious introduction, the first movement dances in a lilting dotted rhythm. The Allegretto, built on a steady, processional pattern (long-short-short-long-long), was encored at the premiere and became one of Beethoven’s most popular pieces, often performed separately. The Presto is an exhilarating scherzo with a hymn-like trio, heard twice. The finale is a frenzied, spinning dance that Wagner described as the ‘apotheosis of the dance’. The Allegretto’s processional rhythm and haunting melody have made it one of Beethoven’s most famous movements, used in many films.
92.ctx: The symphony was premiered on 8 December 1813 at the University of Vienna, at a charity concert for soldiers wounded at the Battle of Hanau, alongside Wellington’s Victory. The concert was a huge success, and the Allegretto had to be repeated. Musicians in the orchestra included Spohr, Salieri, Hummel and Meyerbeer. It was dedicated to Count Moritz von Fries. Some critics found its rhythmic insistence excessive; Weber is said to have claimed that Beethoven was ‘ripe for the madhouse’ after hearing it, though this story is doubtful. Beethoven conducted the premiere himself. The symphony was one of his greatest public successes, and it was repeated several times in the following months.

93.about: Beethoven’s shortest and wittiest symphony since the First. It plays with classical forms, with a compact first movement that starts at full speed, a ticking Allegretto scherzando, an old-fashioned minuet with a horn-and-clarinet trio, and a finale full of wrong-key surprises and an extended, joyful coda. The first movement opens without an introduction, its main theme stated forte at once. The Allegretto scherzando ticks steadily in the winds while the strings play a playful melody. The minuet is deliberately old-fashioned, and its trio features the horns and clarinet. The finale is full of surprises, including a sudden C-sharp that eventually leads to F-sharp minor before returning to F major, and its long coda seems to end several times before the final chords.
93.ctx: Beethoven called it his ‘little symphony in F’. When audiences preferred the Seventh, he reportedly said it was because the Eighth was ‘so much better’. The ticking second movement was once linked to the metronome and a canon Beethoven allegedly wrote for its inventor, Johann Nepomuk Maelzel, but the canon is now thought to be a forgery by Schindler. The symphony was premiered on 27 February 1814 in the Redoutensaal in Vienna, in a concert that also included the Seventh Symphony. It was composed in 1812, partly in Linz, where Beethoven was visiting his brother Johann.

95.about: Beethoven’s most compressed and volatile quartet. Its movements are short and full of abrupt contrasts. Beethoven titled it ‘Quartetto serioso’ and wrote that it was ‘for a small circle of connoisseurs’ and not for public performance.
95.ctx: Dedicated to Nikolaus Zmeskall, a close friend and amateur cellist. Its concentrated, experimental style anticipates the late quartets. It was composed in 1810 but not published until 1816.

96.prem: 29 December 1812, Vienna (Pierre Rode, violin; Archduke Rudolph, piano)
96.about: Beethoven’s last violin sonata, intimate and reflective. The first movement opens with a gentle trill, and its lyrical themes flow naturally. The Adagio espressivo is hymn-like, leading without a break into a brief, playful scherzo in G minor with a waltz-like trio. The finale is a set of variations on a folk-like tune, including a surprising Adagio and a fugato.
96.ctx: Written for the French violinist Pierre Rode, whose gentle style influenced the sonata’s character. It was premiered on 29 December 1812 by Rode and Archduke Rudolph, to whom it was dedicated. Beethoven revised it after the premiere, and it was published in 1816. It was composed around the time of the ‘Immortal Beloved’ letter.

97.about: Beethoven’s grandest piano trio. The first movement opens with a broad, noble theme on the piano. The scherzo is playful, with a chromatic, fugal trio. The Andante is a set of serene variations on a hymn-like theme, leading without a break into the finale, a lively rondo ending in a brilliant Presto.
97.ctx: Composed in 1811, the trio was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph, who gave its name. At the premiere on 11 April 1814, Beethoven’s deafness made his playing unreliable, as the composer Louis Spohr recorded in his memoirs. It was one of his last public performances as a pianist.

98.about: The first true song cycle. Six songs, on poems by Alois Jeitteles, express longing for a distant beloved. The songs are linked without breaks, and the first melody returns at the end.
98.ctx: It influenced later song cycles by Schubert and Schumann.

101.about: The first of the late sonatas, a deeply lyrical and innovative work. The first movement opens with a dreamy melody that seems to begin mid-thought, without a clear tonic chord, creating a sense of floating. A march of dotted rhythms follows, full of energy and with a canonic trio. The third movement is a short, yearning Adagio that recalls the first movement’s theme before breaking into a vigorous finale. The finale includes a substantial fugue, a hallmark of Beethoven’s late style, and ends with a triumphant coda. The sonata’s continuous flow and cyclic recall anticipate the late quartets. Beethoven’s markings, such as ‘mit der innigsten Empfindung’ (with the most heartfelt feeling), reveal the intimate character of the work. The finale’s fugue, built on a vigorous subject, anticipates the great fugues of the Hammerklavier and the late quartets. Pianists find the march particularly challenging because of its dotted rhythms and wide leaps.
101.ctx: Composed in 1816 and published in 1817 by Steiner, the sonata was dedicated to Baroness Dorothea von Ertmann, one of the finest interpreters of Beethoven’s piano music. Beethoven called her his ‘Dorothea-Cäcilia’. It was the first sonata where Beethoven specified the German term ‘Hammerklavier’ for the instrument, reflecting his interest in German terminology. The sonata marks the beginning of Beethoven’s late period, after several years of low productivity. Dorothea von Ertmann was a gifted pianist whose playing Beethoven admired; according to Felix Mendelssohn, Beethoven comforted her after the death of her child by improvising for her at the piano.

106.about: Beethoven’s longest and most demanding sonata, the ‘Hammerklavier’ is a monumental work. The first movement opens with a mighty leap and grand chords, and its development includes a complex fugato. The scherzo is brusque and capricious, with a strange trio and a prestissimo passage. The Adagio sostenuto in F-sharp minor is one of Beethoven’s longest slow movements, a profound meditation of great emotional depth, lasting nearly 20 minutes. The finale begins with a searching, improvisatory Largo that leads to a colossal, dissonant three-voice fugue ‘con alcune licenze’ (with some liberties), full of trills, leaps and harmonic clashes. The sonata’s scale and complexity made it a legendary challenge for pianists. The sonata’s four movements are held together by the interval of a descending third, which appears in the themes and key relationships throughout.
106.ctx: Composed in 1817–18 and published in 1819 by Artaria, the sonata was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph. Beethoven told his publisher it would give pianists ‘something to do’ when played fifty years hence. For decades it was considered almost unplayable; Liszt gave one of the first well-known performances in Paris in 1836. Beethoven’s metronome markings, particularly the very fast tempo for the first movement, have been debated ever since. The sonata was written during a difficult period in Beethoven’s life, when he was involved in a legal battle for the custody of his nephew Karl. Its sheer difficulty and scale made it a symbol of Beethoven’s late style, and pianists such as Liszt and Hans von Bülow helped establish it in the concert hall.

109.about: An intimate late sonata in three movements. The first alternates flowing figuration with slow, improvisatory Adagio interruptions, creating a sense of spontaneity. A fierce, concise Prestissimo follows in E minor. The heart of the work is the finale, a set of six variations on a hymn-like theme marked ‘Gesangvoll, mit innigster Empfindung’ (Songful, with the most heartfelt feeling). The variations range from a lyrical waltz to a fugato and a final variation with trills and shimmering figuration, ending with the theme returning in its simplest form. The sonata’s three movements are unusually balanced towards the finale, which lasts longer than the first two together. The theme of the variations is marked ‘Gesangvoll’ (songful), and its return at the end creates a sense of peace. The first movement’s interruptions give the impression of improvisation, while the Prestissimo provides a burst of energy.
109.ctx: Composed in 1820 and published in 1821 by Schlesinger, the sonata was dedicated to Maximiliane Brentano, daughter of Antonie and Franz Brentano, close friends of Beethoven. Antonie Brentano is one of the candidates for Beethoven’s ‘Immortal Beloved’. The sonata was the first of Beethoven’s last three sonatas, written in quick succession. Beethoven wrote the sonata while also working on the Missa Solemnis. It was published by Schlesinger in Berlin in 1821. Maximiliane Brentano, the dedicatee, was only 10 when Beethoven wrote a short piano trio for her in 1812.

110.about: A deeply personal sonata that moves from quiet lyricism to triumph. After a gentle opening and a humorous scherzo, the finale alternates a sorrowful ‘arioso dolente’ lament with a fugue. The lament returns, weaker, marked ‘ermattet, klagend’ (exhausted, lamenting), before the fugue rises again, gathering strength with an inverted subject, into a jubilant close. The first movement is gentle and lyrical, with arpeggios and a songful theme, while the scherzo is abrupt and humorous. The finale’s structure — lament, fugue, lament, fugue — is unique in the sonata literature. The final fugue’s gradual acceleration and the inversion of its subject create a powerful sense of rebirth, and the sonata ends in radiant A-flat major. The repeated notes in the arioso, marked with changing fingerings, suggest a tremulous, sobbing voice.
110.ctx: Composed in 1821–22 and published in 1822 by Schlesinger, the sonata has no dedication. Beethoven had been seriously ill with jaundice in 1821, and many hear the finale’s alternation of lament and fugue as a journey from exhaustion to recovery. The scherzo quotes two popular Viennese street songs, ‘Unsa Kätz häd Katz’ln ghabt’ (Our cat had kittens) and ‘Ich bin lüderlich, du bist lüderlich’ (I’m a slob, you’re a slob). The sonata was composed in 1821–22, the same period as the Missa Solemnis and Op. 111. It is often considered the most personal of the three last sonatas. Beethoven dated the autograph 25 December 1821, and the finale’s structure has inspired much commentary, including by Alfred Brendel.

111.about: Beethoven’s last piano sonata, in only two movements. The first is a fierce C-minor struggle with a dramatic introduction full of diminished-seventh chords and a fugal Allegro con brio ed appassionato. The second, the Arietta, is a set of variations on a simple, hymn-like theme in C major. The variations gradually increase in rhythmic activity, including a famous syncopated variation often compared to jazz or boogie-woogie, before dissolving into trills and high, luminous textures, creating an effect of transcendence. The first movement’s introduction, with its dramatic diminished-seventh chords and double-dotted rhythms, recalls the French overture, while the Allegro’s fugal passages show Beethoven’s interest in counterpoint. The Arietta’s theme is simple, and each variation subdivides the rhythm further, until the music dissolves into trills. Its ending, in C major, seems to leave the struggles of the first movement behind.
111.ctx: Composed in 1821–22 and published in 1823 by Schlesinger, the sonata was dedicated to Archduke Rudolph (the English edition was dedicated to Antonie Brentano). When asked why there was no third movement, Beethoven reportedly joked that he had not had time. Thomas Mann gave the Arietta a famous discussion in his novel Doctor Faustus, in which a lecturer explains why the sonata could have no third movement. The sonata has become a touchstone for pianists. The sonata was the last of Beethoven’s thirty-two, and he never returned to the genre, though he lived another five years. Its two-movement structure has been interpreted as a contrast between struggle and transcendence, or between earthly and spiritual worlds. Pianists such as Artur Schnabel and Maurizio Pollini made celebrated recordings of it.

120.about: One of the greatest sets of variations ever written. From a simple waltz by Anton Diabelli, Beethoven creates 33 variations of immense variety, ranging from parody to profound meditation, ending with a fugue and a graceful minuet.

123.about: One of the greatest settings of the Mass. It is a deeply personal work, with dramatic contrasts, profound expression and vast scale.

At the top of the Kyrie he wrote ‘Von Herzen – Möge es wieder – zu Herzen gehn!’ (From the heart – may it go again – to the heart!).

125.ded: King Frederick William III of Prussia
125.about: Beethoven’s last symphony and one of the pinnacles of Western music. The first movement emerges from bare, open fifths into titanic struggle. The scherzo is thunderous and driving, with famous timpani octaves. The Adagio is a serene set of double variations of great tenderness. The finale begins with a dissonant fanfare, then the cellos and basses reject fragments of the earlier movements in a recitative, before introducing the ‘Ode to Joy’ melody, which grows into a choral hymn to human brotherhood. The finale includes a Turkish march, a double fugue and a jubilant coda. The symphony’s scale and use of voices broke new ground, and its finale is structured like a symphony within a symphony, with an introduction, a scherzo-like march, a slow section and a fugal finale. The ‘Ode to Joy’ melody is deliberately simple, allowing it to be sung by the chorus.
125.ctx: Beethoven was completely deaf at the premiere on 7 May 1824 at the Kärntnertortheater in Vienna. He stood beside the conductor, Michael Umlauf, and at the end the contralto Caroline Unger turned him to face the audience so he could see its applause. The ‘Ode to Joy’ melody is now the anthem of the European Union. The symphony was dedicated to King Frederick William III of Prussia. Its manuscript is listed in UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register. According to legend, the length of the CD was chosen to fit a performance of the symphony. Beethoven had been planning to set Schiller’s poem since his youth in Bonn, and sketches for the symphony date back to 1817. The London Philharmonic Society commissioned the work.

127.about: The first of the late quartets. It opens with grand, majestic chords before a lyrical Allegro. The heart of the work is a set of variations of great depth, with a variety of textures and moods. The scherzo is rhythmic and quirky, and the finale has a folk-like character.
127.ctx: Beethoven’s last five quartets, written after the Ninth Symphony between 1824 and 1826, are among the most profound works in music. Three were commissioned by Prince Nikolai Galitzin, a Russian nobleman and cellist, who offered Beethoven 50 ducats per quartet. The late quartets were considered incomprehensible by many of Beethoven’s contemporaries, but have become touchstones for later composers. The first performance, on 6 March 1825 by the Schuppanzigh Quartet, went poorly, and Beethoven had it repeated with a different violinist, Joseph Böhm.

131.about: A quartet of seven movements played without a break. It opens with a slow fugue of great depth and moves through a wide range of emotions, including a long set of variations, before a fierce finale. Beethoven considered it his greatest quartet.

Stravinsky later called it ‘an absolutely contemporary piece of music that will be contemporary forever’.

135.about: Beethoven’s last complete major work, a compact and classical quartet. The finale is headed ‘The difficult decision’, with a slow question, ‘Muss es sein?’ (Must it be?), answered by a cheerful ‘Es muss sein!’ (It must be!).

2/1.about: The sonata that opens Beethoven’s official canon of thirty-two is a statement of intent: compact, argumentative and in a minor key. Its first theme is a ‘Mannheim rocket’ — a rising arpeggio borrowed from the orchestral style of the day — that snaps off into a tight turn, and the whole Allegro grows from that gesture and its sighing answer, with a terseness that recalls the finale of Mozart’s G-minor Symphony, which Beethoven clearly knew. The Adagio is a gentle, ornamented aria adapted from the Piano Quartet in C, WoO 36, that he had written as a teenager in Bonn, dressed now in more refined figuration. The Menuetto keeps the minor-key shadow, with a flowing F-major trio. The Prestissimo finale is the real surprise: a whirl of pounding triplet chords and hand-crossings, interrupted by a long, calm, song-like episode in A-flat that sounds almost like a different piece before the storm returns. Across the four movements the young composer shows he can think in large spans rather than in pretty episodes — the quality that set him apart from the many pianist-composers competing for attention in Vienna.
2/1.ctx: Beethoven reached Vienna in November 1792 to study with Haydn, supported by the Elector of Cologne and armed with Count Waldstein’s famous send-off. The Op. 2 sonatas were composed across his first years there and published by Artaria in 1796 with a dedication to Haydn, a public courtesy that masked a cooler private relationship; Beethoven had quietly been taking extra counterpoint lessons from Johann Schenk and Johann Georg Albrechtsberger. Choosing to present three large four-movement sonatas — with minuets or scherzos, like symphonies — rather than the two- and three-movement sonatas common at the time was a claim to seriousness. He had already played them in the salons of Prince Karl Lichnowsky, his most important early patron, where Haydn himself is said to have heard them. Several of their ideas were recycled from the Bonn piano quartets, which remained unpublished during his lifetime: an early sign of Beethoven’s habit of never wasting a good idea.
