This is the only Op. 2 sonata in a minor key.

2/2.about: The A-major sonata is the most playful and brilliant of the set, written by a composer who was also a famous virtuoso. The opening Allegro vivace tosses its first theme between registers with wide leaps, then plunges into a surprising excursion to distant keys, while the development builds a stormy passage of broken octaves. At the heart of the sonata is the Largo appassionato in D major, one of the first great slow movements in Beethoven’s piano music: a solemn, hymn-like melody sustained above a bass marked staccato, as if plucked by a cellist, so that the pianist must make one hand sing while the other ‘pizzicatos’. The third movement is Beethoven’s first piano sonata scherzo, quick and witty with a sombre A-minor trio. The finale is a rondo marked Grazioso whose theme opens with a flamboyant upward arpeggio — each return is decorated differently — and whose central episode erupts into a fierce A-minor section with driving triplets, before the grace of the opening returns. The sonata shows Beethoven blending the elegance of the classical style with a new breadth and daring.
2/2.ctx: Written between 1794 and 1795 and published with its companions in 1796, this sonata reflects the young Beethoven’s success as a performer in aristocratic salons, where he was admired especially for his improvisation. Carl Czerny, his later pupil, remembered that Beethoven’s playing was notable for its legato and its power, and the wide-ranging textures of this sonata demand exactly that. The piano of the day — a Viennese instrument by makers such as Anton Walter — had a range of barely five octaves, and Beethoven already writes at its limits. The Largo’s staccato bass shows his interest in imitating orchestral and string effects on the keyboard, a trait that would grow throughout his career. Publishing three such demanding sonatas as his first solo piano works was a bold move for a composer still best known as a pianist.
parts: Playful sonata form full of leaps and sudden changes of direction.
A hymn-like melody over detached, staccato bass notes.
Beethoven’s first piano sonata scherzo: light and quick-witted.
An elegant rondo with a flamboyant opening flourish and a stormy A-minor episode.
facts: The Largo appassionato is Beethoven’s first slow movement to carry the marking ‘appassionato’.
It contains the first movement titled ‘Scherzo’ in his piano sonatas.
Henle lists it at ABRSM Grade 7 level.

2/3.about: The C-major sonata is the most virtuosic of Op. 2 and the one most like a concerto. Its first movement is packed with rapid broken octaves, trills and double thirds, and near the end it stops on a dominant chord for a written-out cadenza, exactly as in a concerto. Its main themes also come from the unpublished Bonn Piano Quartet in C, WoO 36 No. 3. The Adagio moves to the unexpected key of E major, a third away from the home key — an early example of Beethoven’s love of such distant relationships. It alternates a serene, hymn-like theme with a turbulent E-minor section of flowing arpeggios, before a sudden fortissimo return in C major. The Scherzo is built on a playful, imitative figure passed between the voices, and its trio is a stream of broken chords. The finale, Allegro assai, is a brilliant sonata-rondo that opens with rising chord-leaps and runs of sixths, and includes a warm, chorale-like episode before a sparkling close full of trills. It is a showpiece meant to dazzle, but its sense of drama is already distinctively Beethoven.
2/3.ctx: Beethoven’s reputation in his first Vienna years rested on his playing, and this sonata was plainly written to display it. Contemporary accounts describe how he could overwhelm listeners in improvisation contests with rival pianists such as Joseph Wölfl and Daniel Steibelt, and the flourish and bravura of Op. 2 No. 3 reflect that competitive world. Beethoven was studying counterpoint with Albrechtsberger at the time, and the careful imitative writing of the scherzo shows those lessons at work. Pianists have long valued this sonata as a technical study; its demanding passagework made it a staple of nineteenth-century virtuosos, and it remains a favourite in competitions. Henle rates it at level 7, one of the harder early sonatas.
parts: Sonata form in concerto style, with rapid double thirds and a written cadenza.
A deeply felt slow movement with a dramatic E-minor middle section.
A lively, imitative scherzo with a swirling trio.
A brilliant finale of chord leaps and running figures, with a songful middle episode.
facts: The first movement includes a written-out cadenza, a concerto feature rare in a solo sonata.
Its Adagio is in E major, a distant key relative to C major.
Like Op. 2 No. 1, it reuses material from the Bonn piano quartets WoO 36.

10/1.about: The first of the three Op. 10 sonatas is compressed and fiery, one of Beethoven’s ‘C-minor’ works, the key he used for turbulent, heroic music. The opening Allegro molto e con brio slams upward in dotted chords and is answered by a gentle, pleading phrase; this contrast of force and tenderness drives the whole movement, which is lean and full of silences. The Adagio molto in A-flat major is a long, richly ornamented song with a decorated return, in the style of an operatic aria. The finale, a short Prestissimo, is nervous and full of sudden pauses; its development briefly outlines a short-short-short-long rhythm that anticipates the Fifth Symphony, and it ends by fading away in C major rather than in triumph. At only three movements, the sonata shows Beethoven experimenting with concentration rather than scale. Pianists often note how much of the first movement is built on silence: the rests between the explosive chords are as important as the notes, and the tension depends on the player’s nerve in holding them. The two outer movements share a clipped, rhetorical manner, and the long melodic lines of the Adagio stand out all the more by contrast. The sonata is frequently taught as an introduction to Beethoven’s dramatic style because it presents the essentials — motivic concentration, sudden dynamic shocks, and a large emotional arc — within a short span.
10/1.ctx: The Op. 10 set, composed between 1795 and 1798 and published in 1798 by Joseph Eder, was dedicated to Countess Anna Margarete von Browne, wife of Count Johann Georg von Browne, a wealthy Russian officer who was one of Beethoven’s most generous early patrons. Beethoven reportedly received a horse from the count in gratitude for a dedication, which he promptly forgot about. C minor had a special significance for Beethoven: it is the key of the Pathétique Sonata, the Third Piano Concerto, the Fifth Symphony and his last sonata, Op. 111. Scholars often point to Mozart’s C-minor works, especially the Fantasia and Sonata K. 475/457, as a model for this intense, dramatic style. The Op. 10 sonatas were among the first works Beethoven offered to publishers as a composer in his own right rather than as a performing pianist, and the reviews were mixed: the Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung praised their ideas but complained of an overloaded, sometimes bizarre style — a verdict it would repeat about many of his works over the next decade. Ferdinand Ries later recalled Count Browne’s generosity, including the gift of a horse, which Beethoven reportedly forgot about until a large feed bill arrived.
parts: Fierce, rising chords answered by gentle, pleading phrases.
A short, nervous finale that fades away in the major.
facts: Its finale contains an early hint of the Fifth Symphony’s famous rhythm.
Ferdinand Ries recalled that Count Browne once gave Beethoven a horse, which he promptly forgot about.
Henle rates it level 7 (ABRSM ARSM).

10/2.about: The shortest and most humorous of the Op. 10 sonatas, in F major, full of Haydnesque wit. The first movement opens with a teasing, stop-start theme and later famously begins its recapitulation in the ‘wrong’ key of D major before sliding back to F, a joke that only works if the listener expects the classical form. The middle movement, an Allegretto in F minor, is a smooth, shadowy minuet-like piece with a warm, chorale-like trio in D-flat major. The finale, Presto, is a brilliant, contrapuntal romp in which a chattering theme is tossed from voice to voice, like a playful fugue, before closing with a brisk flourish. The sonata’s outer movements are some of the lightest music Beethoven wrote for the piano, but they demand crisp articulation and rhythmic control; the finale in particular exposes every unevenness in the fingers. The middle movement, with its legato lines in the low register and its hymn-like trio, is a subtle study in voicing. Because it has no real slow movement, the work moves quickly from one character to the next, and its charm lies in its unpredictability — phrases that stop short, accents in unexpected places, and a finale that begins as though in the middle of an argument.
10/2.ctx: Composed in 1796–97, this sonata shows Beethoven’s debt to Haydn’s sense of humour, even at a time when his relationship with his teacher was cooling. Czerny described the finale as requiring great lightness and precision. The sonata’s brevity and wit make it a favourite in teaching, but its surprises — the false recapitulation, the sudden dynamic contrasts — demand real understanding of classical form. It was published alongside its two companions in 1798. Many commentators, including Donald Francis Tovey in his companion to the sonatas, have pointed out how much the humour of this sonata depends on the listener’s familiarity with classical conventions: the false recapitulation is funny only if one expects the true one. The late eighteenth-century Viennese audience, steeped in Haydn’s symphonies and quartets, would have caught these jokes immediately. The sonata was published in 1798, the same year Beethoven was increasingly admired as a composer across the German-speaking lands.
parts: Witty sonata form with a mischievous false return in D major.
A dark, legato minuet-like movement with a warm D-flat trio.
A quick finale of chattering imitative entries.
facts: The first movement’s recapitulation begins in D major rather than the home key of F.
It has no true slow movement.
Henle rates it level 7.

10/3.about: The D-major sonata is the most ambitious of Op. 10 and one of the pivotal works of Beethoven’s early career. Its opening Presto is built almost entirely from a four-note descending figure, which Beethoven develops with relentless energy, a technique that would become central to his mature style. The second movement, Largo e mesto (‘slow and sad’) in D minor, is one of the most profound tragic movements Beethoven had yet written: dark chords, sighing phrases, painful dissonances and sudden outbursts build to a climax before the music sinks into a hollow, fragmented close. The Menuetto that follows offers gentle consolation, with a rushing trio of hand crossings. The finale is an eccentric rondo built on a questioning three-note figure, full of pauses and surprises, ending quietly. The Largo is the emotional centre, but the movements around it are carefully weighted to frame it. The Presto’s energy seems almost reckless, the Menuetto’s warmth feels like a return to life after the Largo’s despair, and the finale’s questioning motif, left hanging in pauses, never quite resolves the unease. Pianists find the work technically demanding — the first movement requires fast octaves and wide leaps — but the real challenge is sustaining the Largo’s long, slow tension without letting it fall apart.
10/3.ctx: Anton Schindler, Beethoven’s secretary in later life, claimed that Beethoven said the Largo depicted the state of mind of a melancholic, with all the nuances of light and shade — though Schindler’s reports are often unreliable, the description fits. Czerny called this sonata one of Beethoven’s greatest early works. Composed in 1797–98, it came at a time when Beethoven was beginning to experience the first signs of the deafness that would haunt him. Henle uses this sonata as its example of level 7 difficulty. Composed in 1797–98, the sonata belongs to the years when Beethoven was consolidating his reputation in Vienna while beginning to notice the ringing in his ears that he would describe to friends in 1801. Czerny and later writers regarded it as the most important of the early sonatas after the Pathétique. It has been championed by pianists from Artur Schnabel, whose 1930s recordings of all thirty-two sonatas were the first complete set, to modern interpreters.
parts: A driving movement built almost entirely from its opening four-note figure.
A grief-stricken lament with painful dissonances and sudden outbursts.
A gentle minuet with a rushing, hand-crossing trio.
A playful rondo that keeps asking a three-note question.
facts: Henle uses this sonata as its reference example for level 7.
The Largo e mesto is often considered Beethoven’s first great tragic slow movement.
The first movement is built almost entirely from its opening four-note motif.

14/1.about: An intimate, lyrical sonata in E major, in three movements. The first movement opens with a gentle rising fourth and flowing overlapping voices, like a conversation between string players. The middle movement, an Allegretto in E minor, is wistful and restless, with a C-major trio. The finale is a flowing rondo, Allegro comodo, with running triplets and a lively C-major episode. Its transparent textures and close imitation between voices make it feel like chamber music, which is why Beethoven arranged it for string quartet. The work is a study in understatement. There are no great climaxes; instead, Beethoven explores the interplay of voices, the balance between lyricism and motion, and subtle shifts of key. The first movement’s development section moves through several keys without ever becoming dramatic, and the finale’s triplet rhythms give the music a gentle, flowing momentum. It is often recommended as one of the more approachable sonatas for intermediate pianists, though its clarity leaves little room to hide.
14/1.ctx: Composed in 1798 and published in 1799 by Mollo, the two Op. 14 sonatas were dedicated to Baroness Josefa von Braun, wife of the director of the Vienna court theatres. In 1802 Beethoven arranged this sonata for string quartet (Hess 34), transposing it to F major, and wrote to his publisher complaining about poor unauthorized arrangements of his piano works, insisting that only a composer could make such transcriptions properly. This arrangement shows how naturally the sonata’s textures translate to strings. The sonata belongs to the late 1790s, when Beethoven was writing a great deal of chamber music, including the Op. 12 violin sonatas and the Op. 18 quartets. The string quartet version, made in 1801–02, is sometimes performed today and offers a rare glimpse of Beethoven translating his own keyboard textures into another medium. The Op. 14 pair were among the first of his sonatas to become popular with amateur pianists.
parts: A gentle, lyrical movement with overlapping voices.
A wistful, minuet-like movement with a C-major trio.
A flowing, good-humoured rondo with running triplets.
facts: Beethoven arranged it for string quartet in F major (Hess 34).
Henle lists it at ABRSM Grade 8 level.
The Op. 14 sonatas were dedicated to Baroness Josefa von Braun.

14/2.about: A cheerful, lighthearted sonata in G major, also in three movements. The first movement plays tricks with its rhythm, with syncopations that obscure where the downbeat lies. The middle movement is a set of variations on a crisp, march-like theme in C major, with each variation adding more ornamentation. The finale is a humorous rondo labelled Scherzo, full of rhythmic surprises and ending with a pianissimo joke. Its wit and transparency make it a favourite among students. The first movement’s syncopated opening, which seems to begin on a weak beat, keeps the listener guessing about the meter, a trick Beethoven would use again in later works. The variations on the Andante theme are straightforward but charming, each adding a new layer of rhythmic activity. The Scherzo finale, despite its title, is a rondo full of rhythmic displacement and ends with a quiet, deadpan cadence — a joke that works only when played with complete seriousness.
14/2.ctx: Schindler claimed that Beethoven described the Op. 14 sonatas as dialogues between a man and a woman, or lovers — the first movement of this sonata as a conversation between a pleading and a resisting voice. Whether true or not, the idea reflects the conversational character of the music. The sonata was published in 1799 alongside its companion. The sonata was composed in 1799 and published in the same year. It was one of the first of Beethoven’s sonatas to enter the teaching repertoire, and it remains a favourite for students because of its clear textures and moderate difficulty. Its humour and conversational style reflect the influence of Haydn, whose piano sonatas and trios Beethoven knew well.
parts: Genial sonata form with rhythmic sleight of hand.
Variations on a staccato, march-like theme.
A rondo in scherzo style that ends with a pianissimo punchline.
facts: Its finale is titled Scherzo but written in rondo form.
Schindler reported Beethoven describing the Op. 14 sonatas as dialogues between two characters.
Henle lists it at ABRSM ARSM level.

27/1.about: The first of the two sonatas Beethoven titled ‘Sonata quasi una fantasia’, meaning ‘sonata almost like a fantasy’. Its four movements are played without breaks, and the Adagio’s theme returns before the end. The opening Andante is simple and gentle, framing a sudden lively Allegro. The second movement is a shadowy scherzo in C minor of rolling triplets. The third, a short Adagio con espressione in A-flat, leads directly into the finale, a lively Allegro vivace that recalls the Adagio before a quick Presto coda. The work is improvisatory and continuous, a significant step towards Beethoven’s later unified designs. The sonata is less well known than its companion, but it is a remarkable experiment. The first movement’s simple Andante theme frames a sudden, boisterous Allegro, creating a sense of spontaneity. The scherzo’s rolling triplets and syncopations are full of energy, while the Adagio’s short, songful melody seems to grow naturally into the finale. The return of the Adagio theme near the end of the finale, before the Presto coda, creates a cyclic connection that would become important in Beethoven’s later works.
27/1.ctx: Composed in 1800–01 and published in 1802 by Cappi, the sonata was dedicated to Princess Josephine von Liechtenstein. Beethoven was experimenting with form at this time, and the continuous structure of Op. 27 anticipates his later works, such as the late sonatas and quartets. Henle rates this sonata at level 8, higher than its famous companion. Beethoven’s use of the title ‘quasi una fantasia’ suggests that he wanted listeners to hear these sonatas as freer, more improvisatory pieces than traditional sonatas. This reflects his reputation as a great improviser, and the continuous structure anticipates later works such as the Piano Sonata Op. 101 and the String Quartet Op. 131. The sonata was published in 1802 alongside the Moonlight Sonata.
parts: A simple, gentle theme framing a sudden, lively Allegro.
A shadowy scherzo of rolling triplets.
A short, songful Adagio leading directly into the finale.
A lively finale in which the Adagio theme returns before a quick coda.
facts: The Adagio theme returns in the finale, a cyclic idea.
The movements are played without breaks.
Henle rates it level 8, higher than the Moonlight Sonata.

27/2.about: The most famous of all Beethoven’s sonatas, the ‘Moonlight’ is a masterpiece of mood and structure. It begins with its slow movement: a hushed, rocking triplet accompaniment beneath a sparse, repeated-note melody, played with the dampers raised throughout (‘senza sordino’), creating a hazy, sustained sonority. A graceful Allegretto in D-flat major follows, which Liszt described as ‘a flower between two abysses’. The finale, Presto agitato, is one of Beethoven’s most intense movements, a tempestuous sonata-form storm of surging arpeggios and sharp accents. The sonata moves from stillness to fury, reversing the usual classical order and placing its weight at the end. The first movement’s effect depends on a delicate balance between the steady triplet accompaniment, the slow-moving melody and the sustained bass. The Allegretto, a gentle minuet with a slightly syncopated trio, provides relief. The Presto agitato is a fully developed sonata-form movement with a dramatic, virtuosic character and a brief recitative-like passage near the end. The sonata’s design, which places its most dramatic movement last, was highly influential. It is among the most recognisable pieces of classical music, used in films, advertisements and popular culture.
27/2.ctx: The nickname ‘Moonlight’ came in 1832, five years after Beethoven’s death, when the poet and critic Ludwig Rellstab compared the first movement to moonlight on Lake Lucerne. Composed in 1801 and published in 1802 by Cappi, the sonata was dedicated to Countess Giulietta Guicciardi, a young pupil with whom Beethoven was briefly in love; she married Count Wenzel Robert von Gallenberg in 1803. Czerny reported that Beethoven was irritated by the popularity of the first movement, remarking that he had written better things. The sonata’s popularity grew throughout the nineteenth century, and the ‘Moonlight’ nickname became universal. It was one of the pieces that made Beethoven a household name among amateur pianists, and it remains one of the most frequently performed and recorded of all classical piano works. Its first movement is often played on its own, though the whole sonata is more satisfying as a dramatic journey.
parts: Rocking triplets beneath a quiet, repeated-note melody, to be played with the dampers raised.
A delicate minuet-like interlude — ‘a flower between two abysses’, as Liszt put it.
A tempestuous sonata-form finale of surging arpeggios and sharp accents.
facts: The nickname dates from 1832, after Beethoven’s death.
Beethoven asked for the first movement to be played with the dampers raised throughout.
Henle lists it at ABRSM ARSM level.

31/1.about: The G-major sonata is Beethoven’s most openly comic piano work. In the first movement the right hand repeatedly arrives a fraction before the left, as if the pianist cannot coordinate, and the second theme appears in the ‘wrong’ key of B major — a bold harmonic stroke disguised as a joke. The music moves in jerky starts and stops, with sudden pauses and abrupt shifts of register. The Adagio grazioso is a long, deliberately over-decorated aria in 9/8 time, with trills, runs and cadenzas that parody the florid Italian opera style Beethoven had studied with Salieri; beneath the irony it is also genuinely beautiful. The finale is a relaxed, songful rondo whose coda plays games with tempo, stopping and restarting several times, alternating Adagio fragments with a Presto dash to the end. The sonata is a reminder that Beethoven’s ‘new path’ was not only about drama but also about wit, and that he could make jokes out of the very building blocks of musical form.
31/1.ctx: In 1802, according to Czerny, Beethoven told his friend Wenzel Krumpholz that he was not satisfied with his previous works and would from now on take a ‘new path’. The three Op. 31 sonatas, composed that year, are often seen as the first fruits of this resolution, alongside the Op. 34 and 35 variations. They were commissioned by the Zurich publisher Hans Georg Nägeli for a series called Répertoire des Clavecinistes. When the first edition of this sonata appeared in 1803, it contained numerous errors and even four bars added by Nägeli to ‘correct’ what he thought was a mistake; Beethoven was furious and had Ries prepare a corrected edition with Simrock in Bonn, marked ‘Édition très correcte’. The year 1802 was also the year of the Heiligenstadt Testament, the letter in which Beethoven confessed his despair over his deafness — yet the music of this sonata shows no sign of it.
parts: Deliberately ‘out of sync’ hands and abrupt key shifts.
An elaborately decorated, tongue-in-cheek operatic aria.
A good-natured rondo with a teasing, stop-start coda.
facts: The Zurich publisher Nägeli added four bars of his own, infuriating Beethoven.
A corrected edition was published by Simrock as ‘Édition très correcte’.
The second theme of the first movement is in B major, an unusual key relationship for a G-major sonata.

31/2.about: The D-minor sonata is one of Beethoven’s most dramatic and innovative. The first movement begins with a slow, questioning arpeggio in Largo, followed by an agitated Allegro; these contrasting tempos alternate throughout, blurring the line between introduction and main theme. At the start of the recapitulation, the arpeggio returns and dissolves into a haunting, pedalled recitative — a wordless vocal line that sounds as if a voice were speaking from far away. The Adagio in B-flat major is noble and hymn-like, with drum-like rumbles in the bass and gentle, ornamented melodies. The finale, Allegretto, is a flowing perpetual motion in 3/8 built on a single rhythmic figure, which Czerny said was inspired by a horse galloping past Beethoven’s window. Its persistent motion and melancholy tone create a hypnotic effect, and it ends quietly, fading into silence. The sonata’s use of recitative and its unusual structure made it a landmark in the development of the Romantic sonata.
31/2.ctx: The nickname ‘Tempest’ comes from Anton Schindler, who claimed that when he asked Beethoven about the meaning of this sonata and the ‘Appassionata’, Beethoven replied, ‘Just read Shakespeare’s Tempest.’ Schindler’s reports are often unreliable, and scholars doubt this story, but the name has stuck because it suits the music’s turbulent character. The recitative passages, with their long pedal markings, were so unusual that later editors often changed Beethoven’s pedalling, believing it to be a mistake. On the pianos of Beethoven’s time, which had less sustain than modern instruments, the effect would have been less blurred. The sonata was published in 1803 by Nägeli, alongside Op. 31 No. 1.
parts: Hesitant arpeggios alternate with urgent drive; recitative passages speak without words.
A serene movement with drum-like rumbles in the bass.
A continuous, whirling finale said to have been inspired by a galloping horse.
facts: The ‘Tempest’ nickname comes from a doubtful anecdote by Schindler.
Beethoven’s long pedal markings in the recitatives were often ‘corrected’ by later editors.
Henle lists it at ABRSM LRSM level.

31/3.about: The E-flat sonata is genial and humorous, with no true slow movement. The first movement begins with a questioning phrase on a dissonant chord, as if the music were starting mid-conversation, and it gradually finds its way to the home key. Its lively second theme and brilliant passagework give it a sunny character. The second movement is a scherzo in 2/4 time, staccato and full of dry humour, with an unusual sonata-form structure. The third is a gentle, songful minuet with a chordal trio — the last minuet Beethoven wrote in a piano sonata. The finale, Presto con fuoco, is a galloping tarantella-like movement in 6/8 that suggests a hunt, giving the sonata its nickname ‘La Chasse’ (The Hunt). The work’s charm and energy make it a favourite among pianists.
31/3.ctx: Composed in 1802, the sonata was published in 1804 by Nägeli, separately from its two companions. The minuet’s theme was later used by Camille Saint-Saëns in his Variations on a Theme of Beethoven for two pianos, Op. 35 (1874). The sonata’s humour and energy show a side of Beethoven often overshadowed by his more dramatic works. The Op. 31 sonatas as a group show Beethoven experimenting with structure and character, paving the way for the Waldstein and Appassionata.
parts: Opens mid-thought, with a question answered by warm cadences.
A staccato scherzo in 2/4 time, full of dry humour.
A gentle, songful minuet with a chordal trio.
facts: The minuet is the last Beethoven wrote in a piano sonata.
Saint-Saëns used the minuet as the theme of his Variations for two pianos, Op. 35.
It has no slow movement.

49/1.about: A short, two-movement sonata for students, gentle and melancholy in G minor. The first movement, Andante, is a tender, flowing piece in sonata form with a lyrical melody over a simple accompaniment. The second movement is a cheerful rondo in G major, with a crisp, dancing theme and contrasting episodes. Although simple, the sonata is written with care and offers a good introduction to Beethoven’s style for young pianists. It demands clear articulation and a singing tone. The Andante’s melody moves mostly in steps over a flowing accompaniment, and the challenge for a young player is to shape its long phrases and keep the left hand quiet. The Rondo’s theme, with its crisp repeated notes and quick turns, rewards clean finger work, and the contrasting episodes introduce simple hand-position changes.
49/1.ctx: Beethoven probably wrote the two Op. 49 sonatas in the late 1790s for his pupils, and never intended them for publication. His brother Caspar Carl, who handled some of Beethoven’s business affairs, sold them to the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie in 1805, which is why they carry an opus number much later than their composition. Henle uses these sonatas as its example of level 3 difficulty. They remain among the most widely taught of all Beethoven’s works. Although small, the Op. 49 sonatas are genuine Beethoven, and pianists such as Artur Schnabel and Wilhelm Kempff included them in complete recordings of the sonatas. They offer students a first taste of his style before tackling harder works.
parts: A tender, flowing movement in sonata form.
A lively rondo with a crisp, dancing theme.
facts: Henle uses Op. 49 as its reference example for level 3.
Beethoven’s brother Caspar Carl sold them to a publisher without Beethoven’s involvement.
Composed around 1797–98, they were published in 1805.

49/2.about: A friendly two-movement sonata that is a staple of piano lessons. The first movement bustles with triplets and has a cheerful, open character. The second is a courtly minuet-rondo, with a graceful theme and contrasting episodes. Its minuet theme became one of Beethoven’s best-known melodies when he reused it in his popular Septet, Op. 20. The sonata’s simplicity and charm make it an ideal introduction to Beethoven’s music. The first movement’s triplet figures require even fingerwork, while the minuet teaches phrasing and poise. Both movements are short enough to be learned quickly, which makes the sonata a popular choice for recitals and examinations.
49/2.ctx: Composed around 1795–96, earlier than its companion, the sonata was published in 1805 without Beethoven’s involvement through his brother. The minuet theme’s reuse in the Septet (1799) shows how Beethoven recycled ideas he liked. Like Op. 49 No. 1, it is used by Henle as a reference for level 3. The minuet’s appearance in the Septet shows that Beethoven valued the tune enough to give it a much larger stage a few years later.
parts: A cheerful movement driven by running triplets.
A graceful minuet-rondo, also used in the Septet.
facts: Its minuet theme also appears in the Septet, Op. 20.
Composed around 1795–96.
Henle rates it level 3.

81a.about: One of Beethoven’s few openly programmatic works. It begins with a three-note horn-call motif to which he wrote the word ‘Le-be-wohl’ (Farewell). The first movement moves from a tender Adagio introduction to an energetic Allegro, with the horn-call motif appearing throughout, including a famous passage where the motif overlaps with itself, creating a ‘clash’ of harmonies that suggests the fading of a departing carriage. The slow movement, Abwesenheit (Absence), is a restless, sighing piece of loneliness. The finale, Das Wiedersehen (Reunion), bursts into the joy of reunion with exuberant cascades, before a quiet, glowing coda. The sonata’s programme is clear, but its music is also carefully structured, with the ‘Lebewohl’ motif shaping all three movements.
81a.ctx: Archduke Rudolph, Beethoven’s pupil and patron, fled Vienna in May 1809 as Napoleon’s army approached, and returned in January 1810. Beethoven dated the movements to match these events, making the sonata a personal diary. Beethoven objected when the publisher Breitkopf & Härtel used the French title ‘Les Adieux’, arguing that ‘Lebewohl’ was a personal farewell while ‘adieux’ was said to a crowd. Henle uses this sonata as its example of level 8 difficulty in its guide, although its product listing rates it level 7. It is one of the few works whose programme Beethoven explicitly acknowledged in the score.

12/1.about: The first of Beethoven’s ten sonatas for piano and violin — he always named the piano first, and the keyboard part is as important as the violin’s. The D-major sonata opens with a bold, unison fanfare before a flowing, lyrical theme. The piano and violin exchange material as equals, a departure from the older tradition in which the violin merely accompanied the keyboard. The middle movement is a set of four variations on a simple A-major theme; the third, in A minor, is stormy and dramatic, while the fourth returns to the gentle mood. The finale is a lively rondo in 6/8 time, with a dancing theme and syncopated accents that give it a rustic flavour. Though modest in scale compared with later works, the sonata already shows Beethoven’s confidence in handling dialogue between two instruments, and its brilliant piano writing reflects his own skill as a performer.
12/1.ctx: The three Op. 12 sonatas were composed in 1797–98 and published by Artaria in 1799 with a dedication to Antonio Salieri, the imperial Kapellmeister, with whom Beethoven was taking lessons in Italian vocal composition. A review in the Leipzig Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung in 1799 found the sonatas ‘learned, learned and always learned’ and full of strange modulations, complaining that they lacked natural melody. The critic admitted the composer was a skilled pianist but found the music overloaded with difficulties. Today these works are admired for their freshness and wit, and for the way they balance the two instruments.

12/2.about: A playful sonata with a lighter texture. The first movement, Allegro vivace, features quick, humorous conversation between the instruments, with a theme that is tossed back and forth. The middle movement, Andante, più tosto Allegretto in A minor, is a wistful, sighing piece, with a melody first given to the piano and then shared with the violin. The finale, Allegro piacevole, is a charming, relaxed rondo with a lilting theme. The sonata’s intimacy and humour make it a delight to play and to hear.
12/2.ctx: Part of Beethoven’s first set of violin sonatas, written as he was establishing himself as a composer in Vienna. The sonatas were likely intended for amateur players as well as professionals, and their publication reflected the growing market for chamber music among the Viennese middle class. The Op. 12 sonatas show the influence of Mozart’s violin sonatas, which Beethoven admired.
parts: A quick, humorous conversation between violin and piano.
facts: Its slow movement is in A minor, the tonic minor.
The finale is marked ‘piacevole’ (pleasant).
It is the shortest of the Op. 12 sonatas.

12/3.about: The most expansive of the Op. 12 set, with a virtuosic piano part. The first movement, Allegro con spirito, is brilliant, with rapid piano figuration and sweeping scales. The Adagio con molt’espressione in C major is one of the most beautiful slow movements of the early violin sonatas, a deeply expressive song. The finale, Rondo: Allegro molto, is energetic and witty, with syncopated rhythms and brilliant passagework.
12/3.ctx: The prominence of the piano reflects Beethoven’s own position as a pianist performing these works. The sonata’s key, E-flat major, was associated with grandeur and nobility in the classical period. The Op. 12 sonatas were among Beethoven’s first chamber works to gain wide circulation.

30/1.about: A gentle, lyrical sonata. The first movement is quietly flowing, with a calm theme and delicate textures. The Adagio is warm and songful, one of Beethoven’s most beautiful slow movements for the combination. The finale is a set of six variations on a simple theme, with varied textures and moods. Beethoven originally wrote a different, more brilliant finale, which he transferred to the ‘Kreutzer’ Sonata.
30/1.ctx: Composed during 1802, the year of the Heiligenstadt Testament, as part of a set of three sonatas dedicated to Archduke Rudolph. The Op. 30 sonatas were published in 1803 by the Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie. This sonata is the least performed of the three but is admired for its subtlety.

30/2.about: The most dramatic and heroic of the violin sonatas before the ‘Kreutzer’. It has four movements: a stormy, march-like first movement in C minor, a lyrical Adagio cantabile in A-flat major, a humorous scherzo with a canonic trio, and a fiery finale with a presto coda. Its C-minor intensity and scale make it one of Beethoven’s most powerful chamber works.
30/2.ctx: Its C-minor intensity places it alongside Beethoven’s other stormy C-minor works of the period, such as the Third Piano Concerto and the Pathétique Sonata. It was composed in 1802 and published in 1803. Many violinists regard it as the finest of the Op. 30 set.

5/1.about: One of the first sonatas to treat the cello as an equal partner to the piano, rather than as a bass accompaniment. It has two movements: a spacious Adagio sostenuto introduction leading to a long and brilliant Allegro, and a lively Rondo. There is no separate slow movement. The piano part is virtuosic, reflecting Beethoven’s own skill as a pianist, while the cello has lyrical and brilliant passages.
5/1.ctx: Beethoven wrote both Op. 5 sonatas during a concert tour to Berlin in 1796, for the court of the cello-playing King Frederick William II of Prussia. He performed them with the court cellist, one of the Duport brothers. The king rewarded Beethoven with a gold snuffbox filled with louis d’or. The sonatas were published in 1797 by Artaria.

102/1.about: A concise, fantasia-like sonata in two parts. Each begins with a slow introduction before a vigorous Allegro. The first Allegro is in A minor, the second returns to C major after a reminiscence of the opening.
102/1.ctx: Written for the cellist Joseph Linke, who played in the household of Countess Erdődy, a close friend of Beethoven. Beethoven called it a ‘free sonata’ (Freie Sonate).

102/2.about: The last of Beethoven’s cello sonatas. A bold, energetic Allegro is followed by a profound slow movement, and the finale is a complex fugue — a hallmark of his late style.

18/1.about: The first quartet in the published set is also its most ambitious. The opening Allegro con brio is built obsessively from a short, turning motif heard in unison at the start; scholars have counted it more than a hundred times in the movement, and Beethoven’s development shows how much drama can be squeezed from a tiny cell. The second movement, Adagio affettuoso ed appassionato in D minor, is a tragic, operatic scene of great intensity, with sobbing figures and violent outbursts, ending in hushed despair. The Scherzo is quick and playful, with a wide-leaping trio. The finale is brilliant and energetic, with running triplets and fugal passages. Together the four movements announce Beethoven as a quartet composer of the first rank, combining Haydn’s motivic rigour with a new emotional intensity.
18/1.ctx: The six Op. 18 quartets, composed between 1798 and 1800 and published in two instalments in 1801, were commissioned by Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz, the music-loving aristocrat who in the same years commissioned quartets from the aging Haydn. Beethoven had long avoided the genre, perhaps intimidated by the achievements of Haydn and Mozart, and he prepared carefully, copying out Mozart quartets and studying counterpoint. The order of publication does not match the order of composition: No. 3 was written first, and No. 1 was substantially revised before publication, as Beethoven wrote to his friend Karl Amenda, asking him not to show anyone the earlier version he had sent him. Amenda later reported that Beethoven, after playing him the slow movement, asked what he thought it depicted; when Amenda answered that it portrayed the parting of two lovers, Beethoven replied that he had imagined the tomb scene from Romeo and Juliet. Beethoven’s sketches for the movement include the French words ‘il prend le tombeau’ and ‘désespoir’ (despair), confirming the Shakespearean connection.

18/2.about: An elegant, witty quartet in a courtly style. The first movement opens with graceful phrases that sound like bows and curtsies, leading to its nickname ‘Komplimentier-Quartett’ (the ‘Compliments’ quartet). The Adagio cantabile in C major is an ornate song that is interrupted by a quick, dancing Allegro middle section, a surprising contrast. The Scherzo is light and witty, with a trio that shifts to C major. The finale is a lively, humorous Allegro molto quasi presto, with a playful theme and sudden changes of key. The quartet’s grace and wit show the influence of Haydn.

The third movement is a graceful, minuet-like Allegro with a minor-key trio. The finale is a brilliant, galloping Presto in 6/8 time, with rapid passagework and surprising harmonic turns.

Instead of a slow movement there is a light, fugal scherzo, Andante scherzoso quasi Allegretto. The third movement is a stormy, accented minuet. The finale is a spirited rondo with a gypsy-flavoured theme and a prestissimo coda.

The first movement is lively and in 6/8 time. The third movement, Andante cantabile con variazioni, is a set of five variations on a simple theme in D major, with a mysterious coda. The finale is fleet and contrapuntal.

It alternates with a carefree, dance-like Allegretto, before the melancholy returns briefly and the dance wins. The earlier movements are lively and conversational.

59/1.about: A vast, symphonic quartet, the longest Beethoven had yet written. The first movement opens with the cello singing a broad theme over a pulsing accompaniment, and unfolds on a scale comparable to the Eroica. The second movement is a strange, humorous scherzo beginning on a single repeated note in the cello. The Adagio molto e mesto in F minor is deeply mournful, and leads directly into the finale, which is based on a Russian folk song.
59/1.ctx: Count Andrey Razumovsky, the Russian ambassador in Vienna and a keen amateur violinist, commissioned the three Op. 59 quartets in 1805 and asked Beethoven to include Russian themes. The quartets were completed in 1806 and published in 1808. Razumovsky maintained a private string quartet led by Ignaz Schuppanzigh, which premiered them. The quartets were so novel that musicians at first found them baffling; a contemporary review described them as ‘long and difficult’ and ‘not comprehensible to everyone’. A cellist, reportedly Bernhard Romberg, is said to have stamped on the part of the second movement, thinking it a joke. Beethoven wrote on a sketch for the Adagio, ‘A weeping willow or acacia tree over the grave of my brother’, possibly referring to his brother’s death in childhood.

The Molto adagio is a sublime, hymn-like meditation, marked ‘Si tratta questo pezzo con molto di sentimento’ (to be played with much feeling). The third movement uses a Russian theme in its trio, the same tune later used by Mussorgsky in Boris Godunov. The finale gallops in the ‘wrong’ key of C major before settling in E minor.

1/1.about: The first of Beethoven’s official opus numbers is a genial, confident trio in E-flat major. The opening Allegro begins with a rising arpeggio, the ‘rocket’ gesture that would recur in Op. 2 No. 1, and unfolds with wit and energy, sharing ideas between all three instruments. The Adagio cantabile in A-flat major is a warm, songful slow movement with long, flowing melodies for the violin and cello over a rippling piano accompaniment. The Scherzo, Allegro assai, is lively and imitative, beginning quietly in the ‘wrong’ key before finding its way home. The finale, Presto, opens with a playful, leaping theme — a tenth leap in the piano that became a signature of the movement — and races to a brilliant end. The trio shows Beethoven’s mastery of chamber textures and his gift for combining humour with substance, while giving the piano a leading role that reflects his own skill.
1/1.ctx: Beethoven chose piano trios for his official Op. 1, published by Artaria in 1795 by subscription, with Prince Lichnowsky and many Viennese aristocrats among the subscribers. The trios had been performed at Lichnowsky’s palace, reportedly in Haydn’s presence, before publication. The subscription was a great success and earned Beethoven a substantial sum, launching his career as a published composer. Four-movement trios were unusual at the time — Haydn’s and Mozart’s trios usually had three — and Beethoven’s choice signalled his ambition to treat the genre as seriously as the symphony. This trio may have been composed as early as 1793, soon after Beethoven’s arrival in Vienna, and revised before publication.

The eerie slow movement, Largo assai ed espressivo in D minor, with shuddering tremolos, dark harmony and a mysterious atmosphere, gave the trio its nickname ‘Ghost’. The finale is bright and energetic.

The trios were published in 1809 by Breitkopf & Härtel.

WoO59.about: One of the most famous pieces of music ever written. The gentle, rocking A-minor theme, built on a quiet oscillation between E and D-sharp, alternates with two contrasting episodes: a sunny one in F major with flowing figuration, and a stormy one over a repeated bass note. The piece is in rondo form (ABACA), and its main theme is instantly recognisable. Although it is often taught as an easy piece, the episodes require good technique.
WoO59.ctx: The piece was published forty years after Beethoven’s death by Ludwig Nohl, who read the manuscript’s dedication as ‘Für Elise am 27 April zur Erinnerung von L. v. Bthvn’. Many scholars believe it was intended for Therese Malfatti, a pupil to whom Beethoven proposed marriage in 1810, and that Nohl misread ‘Therese’. Others have suggested Elisabeth Röckel, a singer. The manuscript has been lost. Beethoven revised the piece in 1822 for possible inclusion in a set of bagatelles.
facts: The original manuscript is lost.
The dedicatee may have been Therese Malfatti or Elisabeth Röckel.
Beethoven revised it in 1822.

WoO80.about: A compact set of 32 variations on an eight-bar theme over a descending chromatic bass, in the tradition of the Baroque chaconne. The variations are brilliant and diverse, and the work ends with an extended coda.
WoO80.ctx: Beethoven reportedly thought little of the piece in later years: according to an anecdote passed down through the Streicher family, on hearing it played and learning it was his own, he exclaimed, ‘Oh Beethoven, what an ass you were!’ He never gave it an opus number. It has nonetheless remained a popular showpiece.
facts: Beethoven reportedly disowned it in later years.
It is based on a chaconne-like bass.
Henle rates it level 7 (ABRSM ARSM).

WoO57.about: A gracious, singing rondo in F major, with a warm and flowing melody.
WoO57.ctx: Originally written as the slow movement of the ‘Waldstein’ Sonata, Op. 53. A friend told Beethoven that the sonata was too long, so he replaced it with a shorter introduction and published this movement separately. The name ‘favori’ came from its popularity. Ferdinand Ries recalled learning it by ear after Beethoven played it to him, then playing it to Prince Lichnowsky, who in turn played it to Beethoven as his own composition. Beethoven was so annoyed that, Ries said, he never played for him again.
facts: It was originally the slow movement of the Waldstein Sonata.
Its name ‘favori’ reflects its popularity.
Henle rates it level 6.

WoO39.about: A short, single-movement piano trio in the form of a gentle Allegretto.
WoO39.ctx: Written for the young Maximiliane Brentano, to encourage her piano playing. She later received the dedication of the Sonata Op. 109.

WoO81.about: A brief, lively Allemande in A major for piano.
WoO81.ctx: Sketched early in Beethoven’s Vienna years and revised much later; it was published long after his death.
facts: It is one of Beethoven’s shortest piano pieces.
It was revised in 1822.
It was published posthumously.

WoO134.about: Four different settings of Goethe’s poem ‘Nur wer die Sehnsucht kennt’ (Only one who knows longing).
WoO134.ctx: Beethoven published all four together, a rare chance to hear him try different solutions for the same text.
facts: The poem comes from Goethe’s novel Wilhelm Meister.
Schubert and Tchaikovsky also set this poem.
Beethoven published all four settings together.
